#9395. Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in New York

Christie's auctioneer Yü-Ge Wang sells the top lot of the sale auction house's 19 November auction in New York, Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads) (1983) Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

Price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a new home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

Gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in New York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime New York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.)

Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and important champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd

The evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.)

Apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca said. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

With estates and collections accounting for some of the season’s biggest consignments, auction houses are betting wealthy collectors will shrug off market volatility

Despite the underwhelming result, the sale notched new auction records for Barkley Hendricks and Alma Thomas

New auction records were set for Pollock, Rothko, Brancusi, Miro and Neel

Swan song of veteran auctioneer Jussi Pylkkänen made $640.8m—the house's highest total for a non-single-owner sale in six years

#9394. Heipi’s Hybrid Tripod Head Quickly Swaps Between Ball, Fluid, and Gimbal Head Modes

Heipi’s Hybrid Tripod Head Quickly Swaps Between Ball, Fluid, and Gimbal Head Modes

With more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand. Heipi’s new 2-in-1 hybrid tripod head for photo and video promises the best of both worlds.

Photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable. By loosening the head, photographers can quickly recompose their shots. However, ball heads are not as easy to control or as smooth for panning motion as a traditional pan-tilt fluid head, which videographers typically prefer. Further, Heipi says its new head also delivers the balancing performance of a gimbal head, a popular choice for wildlife and birding photographers with huge, heavy lenses.

“Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred. During a single shoot, creators may switch between wide-angle and telephoto lenses, move from still photography to video, and capture a wider range of perspectives and moments,” Heipi writes on Kickstarter. “Yet different shooting needs often call for different support equipment: a ball head, a gimbal head, a fluid head, and more. Carrying multiple heads adds bulk to your gear and extra weight to every journey.”

Heipi believes its new hybrid head offers all the benefits of separate tripod heads in a single package.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head weighs 560 grams (just over 1.2 pounds) and is about the size of a traditional ball head. However, it can instantly switch from ball head mode to pan-tilt mode, and videographers can screw on a grip for even more control.

Heipi’s new tripod head also features a stepless counterbalance system designed for gear weighing from 1.5 to 5 kilograms (3.3 to 11 pounds). That encompasses a wide range of equipment, including those big, heavy supertelephoto lenses mentioned earlier.

The KB50 features a standard 3/8″-16 UNC female thread on its base, allowing it to attach to a wide variety of tripod legs. It also includes an Arca-Swiss clamp.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $428, which is a $120 discount compared to the $548 MSRP. Heipi says it will begin shipping in April 2027. With just over 40 days left in the campaign, Heipi has already shattered its $10,000 goal.

#9393. Meet AI 2027 Conference (Dec 1)

Juggling between three languages on a daily basis, Iris is known for her love of linguistics, arts, web design and typography, as well as her goldmine of … More about Iris ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

AI is changing how we design and build, and it isn’t slowing down. On December 1, 2026, SmashingConf is hosting the AI 2027 Conference, a live online half day event to take stock of where AI stands today, what we can expect in 2027, and where teams are getting it right.

With AI maturing, it’s clear we need to learn how AI can elevate your workflow as a UX designer and Design System engineer. Most of us are still figuring it out and trying to work smarter in this new world, so we invited industry experts who have been doing this for a while. They show their experience and tell you what works and what doesn’t, so you don’t have to figure it all out yourself.

Every session is practical. Speakers show how they actually work: their tools, their setups, and the small things that are easy to miss. The event ends with moderated breakout rooms, where you can bring your own workflow questions. See you there?

This conference is dedicated to designers and engineers (front-end, UI, UX) who want to understand how AI can improve the way their team works, without the hype. If you’re interested in AI-ready design systems, AI and Figma, harness engineering, agentic AI UX patterns, and AI workflows for design and engineering teams, this conference is right up your alley!

Showing, not telling: All sessions will be highly practical, focusing on how to integrate AI in your daily work and what to expect in 2027.

For our AI 2027 Conference, your friendly host Vitaly will welcome you and quickly explain how the event will run. We can’t wait to meet you!

AI is moving fast. With it come new workflows in product teams, new design patterns, new user expectations and new ways of thinking about building and designing for AI.Let’s look at where things stand today. A lot changed in 2026, and there are things we can now design and build that simply weren’t possible a year ago. We’ll cover the patterns taking shape heading into 2027, from multi-modal experiences to accessibility, and what tends to go wrong along the way. A big part of that is designing for trust, so people feel confident using what we make.What makes AI products reliable in practice? We’ll look at how teams cut down on hallucinations with better context, a well-built harness and sensible guardrails. Then we’ll finish with what’s coming in 2027, including new experiments, regulations and a few takeaways to bring back to your team.Roll up your sleeves for a packed session, full of real-life examples and design patterns.

Great AI-powered products live at the intersection of engineering depth, design craft and product thinking. In this talk, Anna Arteeva shows how to build real, working AI experiences, not just one-shot prototypes that fall apart the moment someone uses them.You’ll learn how to design and prototype an AI-powered experience from scratch, with functionality built on LLMs, voice and image generation logic. Anna will also show how to add that little bit of delight to your app, and how it can respond to different types of input, whatever the person on the other side of the screen gives you: text, voice or images.

What coding agents need from your design system docs, and how to write it.Documentation is the part of the design system teams are least happy with, and it’s been that way for years. Luke Murphy looks at how we ended up with docs nobody reads and why agents change the picture. Then, drawing on DS ARC’s tests of real design systems, he walks through the small writing changes that make docs work for agents and people alike.This is a talk from our friends at zeroheight. Thank you for joining in!

The big question for many teams is how to get your code and your Figma file talking to each other. In this session, Christine Vallaure shares how she has set this up in practice: going from code to Figma instead of the other way around, moving back and forth between the two for the best result, and what that means for how we work.You’ll hear why design system basics suddenly matter a lot more, why naming things well pays off, and why AI builders so often produce code that looks like your design system but still has to be rebuilt. She’ll also explain the engineering side that designers don’t always see, like the checks and files your developers set up, so you know how it works and what to ask for. Along the way, she covers the problems you’re likely to run into, what to keep in mind, and where Storybook fits in.Expect plenty of small tips and tricks you can take straight back to your team.

AI flipped the script on the traditional, linear design system workflow. That’s okay. We’re all experimenting, and nobody has this figured out yet.TJ Pitre has spent the past two years working with dozens of teams to find the flow that fits them. He’ll show three alternative workflows live. Which one fits depends on you: how big your design system is, how big your team is, how much effort you’re willing to put in, and how well it needs to scale.The goal is to get you thinking, and to send you back to your team with a few workflows worth trying.

Brad Frost shares his actual workflow for building products with AI and a design system. He’ll show the setup, architecture, and tools he uses to keep AI on the rails of his components, tokens, and patterns.Expect live building, real design decisions, and plenty of practical tricks along the way. You’ll see how it all works together and leave with ideas to apply to your own design system and workflow.

Designing & Building AI Experiences in 2027The way we design and build is changing massively, and we are all adapting to the new reality. In this session, we’ll talk about how to design and build AI experiences that actually work, and are a delight to use. Bring your questions, post your problems and work with Vitaly and Anna, and all the other attendees, to solve them together. We’ll look at everything from interaction patterns and prototypes to adding those little touches of delight, and have some fun while doing it!Have a specific UX AI problem? Ask it in the Google doc, and get your question answered!

Design Systems & AI in 2027Let’s be honest: work is messy. But let’s see how we can make it work, and have some fun while doing it! Ask all your questions, post your problems and work with Christine, Brad & TJ, and all the other attendees, to solve them together.Have a specific design system headache? Bring your questions, and let’s discuss!

We will be emailing you with the video recordings, the slides, the collaborative docs, the takeaways and more. Everything in one place, so you can rewatch the talks you loved and catch the ones you missed.

We’ll open the doors 15 minutes early! Make sure to check your timezone 🌍 so you make it on time. We look forward to seeing you there!

On December 1, 2026, you’ll get to learn from and share your UX AI problems and design system headaches with six experts: they’re all very excited to share their personal practical tips, clever tricks and valuable insights that you can put into action right away. Expect plenty of inspiration, useful takeaways, and, of course, a little fun along the way!

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing or speaking at a conference, he’s most probably running front-end/UX workshops and webinars. He loves solving complex UX, front-end and performance problems.

Anna Arteeva is a product design leader turned agentic coding instructor, and one of Maven’s top-ranked educators, formerly head of product design at Payoneer. With a technical background (frontend), a career in product design, and a healthy obsession with building things. She found her calling in helping designers unlock their superpowers with coding agents, helping designers move beyond AI hype and one-shot prototypes, and develop the technical fluency, practical skills, and good judgement to make agentic coding a powerful part of professional design practice.

Christine Vallaure is a designer and educator with twenty years in product work. She is the founder of Moonlearning.io, a learning platform that helps designers blur the line between design and code, and the author of The Solo. Christine spends most of her time in the developers’ weeds and brings back what designers actually need, then turns it into far too detailed articles, hands-on teaching and talks at conferences around the world.

TJ Pitre is the Product Architect for AI and Design Systems at Figma, and Founder/Owner of Southleft, a design systems consultancy. He works with teams to bridge design and engineering using structured context, modern tooling, and practical experimentation.

Brad Frost is a design system consultant, web designer & developer, speaker, writer, teacher, musician, and artist located in beautiful Pittsburgh, PA. He helps people establish & evolve design systems, establish more collaborative workflows, and design & build software together. Brad is the author of the book Atomic Design, which introduces a methodology to create and maintain effective design systems. He co-hosted the Style Guides Podcast and has helped create several tools and resources for web designers, e.g. an online course, AI & Design Systems, with experts from the industry.

We’re excited to have our friends at zeroheight on board. The folks at zeroheight have created a platform for creating, managing and publishing design system documentation. Designers and developers get to work in the same place, so docs are more than a handoff. Find out more at zeroheight.com.

Join zeroheight’s Principal Design Advocate Luke Murphy for a partner talk on why nobody reads your design system documentation, and what coding agents need from your docs. (Thank you for joining in, dear Luke!)

With a commitment to quality content for the design community.

#9391. The Associated Press is Moving Eight US Photo Editor Jobs to India

The Associated Press is Moving Eight US Photo Editor Jobs to India

The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.

The roles are currently carried out in the United States, but today is their last day. The offshoring follows similar moves this summer, when AP laid off 20 video production jobs in the U.S. and moved them to its hub in Noida, India.

“AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week. “The News Media Guild learned Monday that AP will offshore eight photo positions after already gutting its U.S. video production team.”

In a statement, the News Media Guild president Kimberlee Krusei called AP’s move “union busting.”

“Fewer people, fewer communities being covered, and less news. That’s the impact of today’s decision,” says Krusei. “AP’s newsgathering has gone beyond ‘lean’ to leaving many coverage areas abandoned. The remaining journalists are asked to do the impossible and it shows.”

The Guild says that far from just picking photos taken by AP photographers, the editors provide direction, guide the photographers, correct essential information, and scrutinize images for alterations.

“They bring decades of local knowledge, news judgment and connections. They negotiate with outside photographers to buy the rights to photos — a now essential part of covering breaking news.”

One of the affected photo editors, Pablo Salinas, who is based in New York, says that he went above and beyond in 2019 when he obtained the rights to a shocking photo of a drowned father and daughter lying face down in the Rio Grande River.

“That was a picture that I don’t think any other photo editor would have been able to get,” says Salinas. “Because it wasn’t ours, I scoured social media and found it and got in touch with the photographer. And she reluctantly gave us permission to use it.”

The photo went viral and became part of the story about the border crisis.

“AP benefits from having photo editors that are local to where the news is being produced,” says AP photographer Matt Rourke.

“It’s a partnership,” adds Salinas. “The kind of partnership you lose when you sacrifice these jobs to save a few dollars.”

Photo editors are intimately involved in the biggest stories of the day. They might be working closely with local photographers to move hundreds of shots illustrating important election results. Or securing the rights to sensitive images that convey difficult news. AP’s Pablo Salinas went in front of the camera to talk about the partnership that’s lost when news leaders sacrifice jobs like his. Tell the company their valuable work can’t just be done from anywhere at this link: https://t.co/euBigYM1tt

— AP News Guild (@APNewsGuild) November 12, 2026

An AP spokesperson tells TheWrap that the agency is respecting and following the collective bargaining agreement.

“This is part of the changes we announced over the summer to significantly scale our visual production capabilities at our new hub in Noida, India, where we have added dozens of talented journalists to our global news organization,” the spokesperson says.

The AP says that its hub in Noida will soon employ nearly 100 video producers and photo editors.

#9388. The Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor Is the Lightest and Most Affordable Prime of Its Kind

The Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor Is the Lightest and Most Affordable Prime of Its Kind

Thypoch has announced its first autofocus prime lens, the $349 AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor for Fujifilm X mount.

Editor’s Note: This article originally appeared on PetaPixel on October 27. Multiple outlets including B&H Photo listed the lens, but Thypoch changed the release date after publication. As a courtesy, PetaPixel agreed to adjust the publish date to November 20. The content of this story is unchanged.

With its approximately 35mm equivalent focal length, Thypoch’s first autofocus lens for Fujifilm X mount and first autofocus prime lens period is well-suited to a wide range of photographic applications. The 35mm focal length is a classic one for a reason. It works well for street, landscapes, portraits, and travel, to name a few go-to genres.

Thypoch has long been associated with classically-inspired manual focus lenses, like the Simera 50mm f/1.4 and Ksana 21mm f/3.5. However, the company’s vibe changed considerably when it launched its first autofocus lens, the Voyager 24-50mm f/2.8 for full-frame Sony E-mount cameras.

The new Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor is styled much like the Voyager, with diagonal lines and a vintage-inspired yet modern design. Although beauty is subjective, the Sculptor will likely earn a few fans thanks to its handsome looks.

It's ultimately what's on the inside that counts, though. Inside the Sculptor, 12 lens elements are arranged across ten groups, promising edge-to-edge sharpness even at the maximum f/1.4 aperture. A 10-bladed aperture diaphragm sits behind the glass.

The lens is also quite compact, measuring just 71.4 millimeters (2.8 inches) long with a 52mm front filter thread. The lens weighs 283 grams (just under 10 ounces).

The autofocus prime can focus as close as 0.25 meters (0.82 feet), giving a maximum magnification of about 0.13x. It's definitely not a macro lens.

The Sculptor's most obvious competitor is Fujifilm's own XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WR lens, which costs $1,049.95. Fujifilm's lens weighs 375 grams (13.2 ounces) and is 77.8 millimeters (3.1 inches) long. Thypoch's new lens is much lighter and more affordable.

Fujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy new on B&HFujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy used on KEH.comSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy new on B&HSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy used on KEH.com

Another competitor is the Sigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN Contemporary. It's $609 right now thanks to a $50 discount and is generally well respected. It weighs 340 grams (12 ounces) and is 76.9 millimeters (three inches) long. Again, heavier than Thypoch's new lens by a decent margin.

#9386. Drone Operator Films Manchester United Training Session and Leaks Video on YouTube

Drone Operator Films Manchester United Training Session and Leaks Video on YouTube

A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with new coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.

Pochettino officially left the U.S. men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United. On Thursday, he oversaw his first training session with Man United’s first-team squad ahead of Sunday’s Premier League game against Liverpool at the club’s Carrington training ground.

However, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session. He then posted a 12-minute segment on YouTube on Thursday.

According to a report by The Athletic, Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, were identifiable in the aerial footage, which amassed over 600,000 views on YouTube. The footage showed Pochettino leading a training session with one group of players, while his assistant Jesus Perez oversaw two separate groups. The video, filmed at United’s Carrington training base, also captured audio of the YouTuber apparently controlling the drone saying “let’s get closer,” before zooming in on the new head coach.

The drone operator has since apologized for a “total error in judgment.” He says the aerial footage was legal under U.K. drone laws but has removed the “unethical” video from YouTube.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Man United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part,” the drone operator writes in a post on YouTube.

The drone operator describes aiming to film Pochettino in the club’s training kit for the first time, but adds he had no intention of recording a “meaningful training session.” The YouTuber says he was operating under an incorrect assumption that it was open to media outlets. He also insists he acted independently and was not working on behalf of Liverpool or any other football club.

“I would like to apologize to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match,” the drone operator says.

Man United prohibits the use of drones at its Carrington training facility, where signs warn that anyone operating a drone could face civil action or prosecution.

#9384. Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia

Five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

The museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

The unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.

This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

The items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia

The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Withdrawn from auction in February, the shield will make a stop at the Toledo Museum of Art before going on public display at the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa

Through the new partnership, the museum is already in the process of returning five artefacts from a private collection to Ethiopian authorities

Westminster Abbey, which is directly under the monarch’s jurisdiction, currently refuses to return the holy tablet

#9381. Photographer Who Hid His Photos Behind Wall Returns to Syria a Decade Later to Find Them

Photographer Who Hid His Photos Behind Wall Returns to Syria a Decade Later to Find Them

A Syrian photographer has finally been reunited with his personal photo archive more than a decade after hiding it behind a wall he built during the country’s war.

Photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar fled Syria more than a decade ago, seeking refuge in Turkey amid widespread destruction, looting, and attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh) and forces loyal to Syria’s now-topled Assad regime, according to a report by Anadolu Agency.

‘Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory’

🇸🇾 Syrian photographer Ahmed al-Bekkar recovers personal archive in Raqqa after more than a decade

● Bekkar, 66, sealed his library before fleeing war to protect books, photographs and personal documents

● He sought refuge in Türkiye amid attacks by Daesh (ISIS) and forces of ousted Syrian regime

— Anadolu English (@anadoluagency) November 19, 2026

Before leaving Syria, Bekkar built a wall to conceal the entrance to his personal library in the northern city of Raqqa, hoping to protect his extensive photographic archive. The archive contains approximately 3,000 printed photographs of Raqqa, as well as a much larger digital collection documenting historical sites, cities, and markets across Syria.

During his decade in Turkey, the now 66-year-old photographer continued his photographic work, helping establish the House of Migrants association and the Turkish-Arab Art House. Although Bekkar spent productive years doing photography in the Turkish capital of Istanbul, he says nothing could replace his hometown in Syria.

Anadolu Agency reports that Bekkar returned to Raqqa this year and reopened the library he had concealed behind the wall more than a decade earlier. The photographer describes watching the bricks being removed one by one from the wall as an emotional experience, having long dreamed of setting foot inside his archive again.

“Every piece of paper has a history, every page holds a memory. I spent time and effort obtaining and preserving every document,” the photographer tells the news outlet. “I feel that those days are preserved in these papers, whose owners are no longer with us, but which have remained behind.”

Bekkar recalled growing up across from an old mosque in Raqqa, where the surrounding historical buildings inspired his interest in photography and Syria’s cultural heritage. Since returning to his hometown, Bekkar has revisited historical sites he photographed years earlier to document them now.

#9379. Save up to $600 on Sony Cameras

Photographers can save hundreds of dollars on an expansive range of Sony mirrorless cameras, from budget-friendly APS-C models all the way to flagship full-frame bodies.

Starting with the APS-C camera deals, photographers can save $50 on Sony’s best APS-C interchangeable-lens model, the a6700. With its 26-megapixel Exmor R BSI CMOS sensor and 4Kp120 recording, the a6700 is a versatile and fully featured camera. While there’s no instant discount on it right now, unlike the rest of the cameras in this story, there is a $50 cashback campaign running through December 31, 2026. The camera is $1,498, but the $50 back later is nice.

With the 24.2-megapixel Sony ZV-E10, which comes in both black and white colorways, the $50 savings is upfront. The video-focused camera, designed for content creators, is $748 thanks to ongoing holiday savings. That's $450 less than its successor, the ZV-E10 II, which costs $1,198 and isn't discounted. That's big savings.

The Sony a6400 isn't quite as advanced as the a6700, but the 24-megapixel model remains a very capable APS-C mirrorless camera. It's also significantly more accessible, especially after its $200 instant holiday discount. At $898, this is among the best values in Sony's APS-C lineup.

On the full-frame side of things, there are a ton of great discounts right now, including up to $600 off a Sony a7 III. While it has been succeeded by the a7 IV and, most recently, the a7 V, the Sony a7 III is still a capable camera, able to capture high-quality 24-megapixel photos and 4Kp30 video. At $1,398 after its $600 discount, it's the most affordable way into a new Sony full-frame camera right now. There's also a $50 cashback campaign for this camera.

Speaking of the newer a7 IV, that's on sale, too. In fact, it's $500 off—plus the $50 cashback campaign. It's $1,998 today before the $50 back later. It has a 33-megapixel sensor, 4Kp60 video recording, and some autofocus bells and whistles its predecessor lacks.

Well, the even newer a7 V is on sale, too! The discount is a bit smaller at just $200, plus $50 back after purchase, but it's still something. The Sony a7 V is great. It missed out on PetaPixel's Camera of the Year Award last year by a single point.

On the other end of Sony's full-frame camera lineup, the former flagship Sony a1 is $5,698 after a $500 discount. Then there's $50 back later with proof of purchase until the end of the year. While the a1 II is naturally an even better camera, a lot of pros are still using the original a1 to do incredible work.

On the topic of the excellent Sony a1 II, that's also on sale. However, even with its $200 discount, it is still $6,798, which is obviously quite a bit more than the original a1. It's an expensive flagship camera, but it is undeniably fantastic. It's the best Sony has to offer.

While the 66-megapixel Sony a7R VI is the talk of the high-resolution town these days, it would be a big mistake to look past its predecessor, the Sony a7R V. The a7R V remains an excellent camera, and at $3,298 thanks to $500 in holiday savings (plus $50 back later), it's a superb value. For reference, the a7R VI is $4,498 before $50 cash back. What are the extra megapixels and added speed worth to you? Landscape and portrait photographers, in particular, may very well find the a7R V more than sufficient.

If you don't like the SLR styling of the a7R V but still want its 61-megapixel image sensor, there's always the a7CR. With its compact form factor and stylish black and silver color choices, the a7CR offers the same image quality as the a7R V without the bulk. It's $400 off and is also part of Sony's cashback campaign. At $2,998, it's an attractive option.

The a7CR's similarly styled sibling, the 33-megapixel a7C II, is $400 off, too. With that discount, it's down to $2,098 right now.

If megapixels don't tickle your fancy but speed does, the Sony a9 III is $400 off for the holidays. Sony's first, and thus far only, global-shutter Alpha camera, the 24-megapixel a9 III is screaming fast. It shoots full-resolution photos with autofocus at up to 120 frames per second, has literally zero rolling shutter, and is built with professionals in mind. It's still $6,398, so the speed doesn't come cheap, but boy, is it ever fast.

The video-focused Sony a7S III might never get a successor, [although we hope it does](https://petapixel.com/2026/09/29/is-a-sony-a7s-iv-coming-fat-chance/), but that doesn't mean the a7S III is bad. Far from it. It remains a great camera for video applications, especially in low-light conditions. It's $3,698 after a $300 discount.

Another video-focused model, the content-creator-friendly ZV-E1, is $300 off right now. Available in black and white colorways, the 12-megapixel camera is very good at video. That discount knocks its price down to $2,198.

While you don't need a Sony memory card for your Sony camera, there are some good deals on Sony Tough cards right now.

The excellent Tough Series UHS-II SDXC memory cards are discounted for the holidays. The 64GB version is $45 off, bringing it down to $133. The 128GB model is $100 off, making it $243. Finally, the 256GB card is $120 off, which means it's $418 right now.

Some of Sony's high-end cameras also use CFexpress Type A cards. A few of those are on sale, too, including $60 off Sony's 960GB CFexpress 4.0 Type A Tough card. It's still $878, though. The 1920GB version is $140 off, which makes it $1,458. Memory card prices have gone wild lately. Unfortunately, the 240GB and 480GB cards aren't discounted right now.

#9377. Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers

Adobe Ends Free Creative Cloud Subscriptions for Stock Photographers

Adobe will no longer offer complimentary Creative Cloud subscriptions to photographers who sell their work through Adobe Stock, replacing the scheme with discounts instead.

For years, Adobe has incentivized photographers to contribute to its picture marketplace by dangling the carrot of a free subscription to Photoshop and other Adobe apps.

Robert Kneschke, a professional stock photographer based in Germany who runs the Daily Life of a Photo Producer blog, says that in 2020, a photographer needed 150 sales to unlock a free Adobe Photography plan, while 5,000 downloads would net them complete access to Creative Cloud.

But Adobe has recently made changes to its bonus program, changing the eligibility and prizes. Instead of offering full complimentary access, Adobe is offering a 70% discount on Creative Cloud Pro to the first 500 contributors who generate 6,500 downloads and submit over 1,000 new images.

The 70% discount is also on offer to the first 500 contributors who “have 10 or more datasets and maintain high quality standards.” It’s not entirely clear what a dataset is from a photographer’s perspective. On its website, Adobe describes it as a “storage and management construct for a collection of data, typically a table, that contains a schema (columns) and fields (rows).”

There’s also a 40% discount on offer for Creative Cloud Pro for the first 10,000 contributors who generate more than 2,500 sales as well as submitting over “100 pieces of unique content.”

The above criteria must be met from September 22, 2026, to March 12, 2027. The codes will be handed out in April.

Adobe will still provide full complimentary access to Creative Cloud Pro to photographers who are “actively commissioned to create content and/or require Adobe tools to fulfill project requirements.”

Writing on his blog, Kneschke calls the changes a “clear step backward” while speculating that the datasets are for AI training purposes.

“A gift has become a discount voucher,” Kneschke says. “Along with the lower royalties, this is further evidence that Adobe is cutting costs at the expense of photographers.”

Earlier this year, PetaPixel reported on Gerald Carter, the owner of Diversity Photos, and his fight with Adobe after he discovered that the company trained its AI image generator Firefly on his entire photo library.

#9375. Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

Sotheby’s New York auction of Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890) on 18 November

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

The auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the New York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890)

Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not announced a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

The uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

Sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

Urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

Comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”

The terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees

As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Three Photographers Sue Police Over Use of Tear Gas and Pepper Spray During ICE Raid

Three photographers have sued the St. Paul Police Department in Minnesota over its alleged use of chemical munitions against them during an ICE raid, with their own photographs documenting the incident.

Warning: The following photos contains content that some may find upsetting.

Aaron Nesheim, a photographer for Sahan Journal, MPR News photojournalist Kerem Yücel, and freelance photographer Timothy Evans filed the lawsuit against the St. Paul Police Department on Tuesday. The photographers accuse officers of firing pepper balls at them, pepper-spraying them at close range, and deploying tear gas against them while they were covering a demonstration.

The lawsuit stems from an incident on November 25 last year, when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents attempted to arrest a man at his home in the Payne-Phalen neighborhood of St. Paul, Minnesota. A growing crowd of protesters gathered outside the property as federal agents attempted to detain the man.

Nesheim, Yücel, and Evans arrived at the scene to document the protest. All three photographers carried large professional cameras and wore press passes around their necks. Evans also wore a ballistic vest labeled “PRESS.”

According to a report by the Minnesota Reformer, St. Paul police officers also responded to the scene. After ICE agents left with the detainees, protesters demanded that local police leave as well. As the officers withdrew, they fired pepper balls and used pepper spray and tear gas against both protesters and photojournalists.

According to court documents, an officer pepper-sprayed Yücel at close range while he was photographing the scene. The lawsuit says that the photographer inhaled and swallowed the chemicals. Other officers fired pepper balls at Yücel, striking him in the neck, shoulders, and chest.

According to the complaint, the three photographers were standing together off to the side of the crowd, at least 10 feet from the nearest protesters and out of the way of law enforcement officers. Despite this, police allegedly fired pepper balls and launched tear gas at the photographers.

All three photographers experienced irritation to their eyes and airways following exposure to the chemicals. Yücel struggled to breathe and was taken from the scene by ambulance. According to MPR News, Yücel was forced to put his jacket into a garbage bag to prevent the chemicals from affecting the crew and staff at Regions Hospital said they could not admit Yücel into the main hospital because the chemical irritants on his body and clothing posed a safety risk to staff and other patients.

Evans suffered severe abdominal bruising after a pepper ball exploded inside his ballistic vest, while Nesheim was struck in the head by a police projectile. All three photojournalists required mental health treatment following the incident.

The photographers argue in their lawsuit that the St. Paul Police Department’s actions violated their rights under the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution and constituted assault and battery, among other violations. They are seeking damages, attorney’s fees, and a court order barring the St. Paul Police Department from engaging in further unconstitutional conduct against them.

“The use of this tear gas, like the use of the pepper balls, was clearly meant as retaliation for plaintiffs’ exercise of their First Amendment rights,”attorney Kevin Riach writes. “The officers could not have been shooting at anyone other than Nesheim, Yücel and Evans, who were all clustered within several feet of one another.”

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Hawaii saver availability on United can be tight, especially during peak travel periods. Here's your playbook:

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

Log into your Miles&Smiles account and search for your United flight to Hawaii. If the online system does not show the award, call Turkish Airlines customer service to book over the phone. Have your flight details and Miles&Smiles number ready.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.
